risks: Hash cohorts may be noisy or arbitrary; users with short histories provide weak cohort evidence; dominant-cohort assignment can separate items used by multiple interests; the additive tangent shift may saturate the ball or distort content geometry. First-level code allocation can leave a parent too few codes.
ideas.safeguards: Hash deterministically with a documented stable hash, use add-one smoothing so no row is empty, resolve all ties by integer ID, and ensure every nonempty parent receives at least one code (merge smallest parents by nearest cohort-mass vector if necessary). Construct P once as a seeded orthonormal projection and normalize Pa_i before mapping; project all ball points to norm <=1-1e-5, clamp acosh inputs to >=1+1e-7, calculate maps/distances in float32 or higher, and use finite checks with safe zero-vector limits. ideas.spec_equations: For training transitions (u,i)->(u,j), hash c(u)=hash(u) mod M. Set h_j[m]=sum_{(u,i,j) in train}1[c(u)=m]; a_j[m]=(h_j[m]+1)/(sum_q h_j[q]+M); g_j=argmax_m a_j[m]. For fixed seeded orthonormal P, b_j=log_0(Pa_j), y_j=exp_0(log_0(z_j)+b_j); q_j=argmin_{k in C_{g_j}}d_{-1}(y_j,c_k)^2. Feed selected first code to the existing straight-through RQ-VAE loss; levels 2 and 3 use the unchanged baseline residual quantizer. Allocate K1 codes by largest-remainder proportional allocation over nonempty parent item counts.
ideas.spec_inputs_outputs: Inputs are Stage2 training user/item sequences, item latents z_i, first-level codebook size K1 and vectors, and run seed. Outputs are frozen user cohort labels, item cohort masses and parent labels, first-level assignments, and complete three-level SIDs with baseline later-level assignments.

specification.text: Deterministically assign each training user to one of M cohorts by hashing their training-only ordered item history into M buckets (M is the existing first-level codebook size, not tuned). For each item i, let h_i[m] be the number of training transitions u: x_{u,t}->i for which user u hashes to m; smooth by one count per cohort and normalize a_i[m]=(h_i[m]+1)/(sum_q h_i[q]+M). Set parent g_i=argmax_m a_i[m] (lowest index breaks ties). Allocate K1 first-level codes across nonempty parents proportional to their item counts by largest remainder, at least one per parent. Let b_i be the Poincare-ball log-map of the normalized cohort-mass vector a_i, after embedding it in the latent dimension with a fixed seeded orthonormal projection P; set y_i=exp_0(log_0(z_i)+b_i). Select q_i=argmin_{k in C_{g_i}} d_{-1}(y_i,c_k)^2, use q_i's code vector in the ordinary straight-through reconstruction update, then perform baseline Euclidean residual quantization for levels 2–3. Fix P from the run seed; no learned behaviour encoder or extra loss weight. The number of interest cohorts is a sixteenth of the first-level codebook size and not the codebook size itself: with one cohort per code every parent receives exactly one code, the restricted argmin is then forced by the parent mask and the curved distance decides nothing, so the mechanism would carry no curved computation on the assignment path at all. With a sixteenth of the codes each parent receives sixteen codes, the curved distance chooses among them, and the parent still determines the first-level behaviour structure. The behaviour displacement is the log map at the origin of the projected cohort-mass vector, which is normalised to a norm of at most 1 - 1e-5 before the map is applied.

ideas.cost_estimate: One sparse transition aggregation and one weighted-embedding barycentre per item are computed once. ideas.motivation: The useful regime appears to require many items to share a coarse first token while retaining item identity in the final token. ideas.novelty: Unlike the other ideas' fixed graph partitions, trees, shells, or behavior-restricted candidate sets, this uses each item's soft successor-flow barycentre as a per-item hyperbolic translation of its latent before one unrestricted global first-level quantizer. ideas.observables: First-level assignments and their gradients should change, with items sharing successor barycentres more often sharing a coarse code; the original-latent residual path should keep third-level triples informative. risks: Successor barycentres may mostly encode popularity or be noisy for rare items; embedding averages can cancel when destinations are heterogeneous; translation may push points near the ball boundary or dominate content; unchanged residual quantization may not recover identity if first-code reconstruction gradients become poorly calibrated.

specification.text: From training transitions define p_i(j)=(n_ij+q_j)/(out_i+1), where q_j is the training-split item unigram probability. ideas.falsifiable_hypothesis: Successor-profile sectors coarsen level 1 around items that serve similar next-item roles; adding the sector prototype before curved assignment causes geodesically nearby codes to encode within-sector semantic variation, while later residual levels preserve item identity. ideas.hyperbolic_location: First-level quantizer assignment; the behavior-conditioned latent and trainable first-level code vectors are mapped into the ball and compared by geodesic distance. Levels two and three remain ordinary residual quantizers so the final token can preserve item identity.
ideas.hyperbolic_operator: Exponential map at the Poincaré origin and squared geodesic distance for fixed negative curvature −κ, with κ derived from the median squared mapped-input scale.
ideas.key_change: Build item sectors by deterministic clustering of training-only, popularity-adjusted successor profiles; allocate contiguous level-1 code IDs to each sector in proportion to its training item mass, with at least one code per sector. At each RQ-VAE update, combine the encoder latent with its training-derived sector prototype, map the result and sector's code vectors to a fixed-curvature Poincaré ball, and select the nearest code geodesically; leave later residual levels as baseline Euclidean quantizers.
ideas.leakage_boundary: Cache q_i, sector labels, sector prototypes, PCA, and code allocation using Stage2 training interactions and training-item embeddings only; freeze those objects before SID export. Stage3 validation/test interactions are not inputs to any SID construction or update.
ideas.motivation: The first SID level should be deliberately coarser and predictive of training next-item flow, while levels two and three retain enough residual capacity to distinguish individual items.
ideas.novelty: Instead of assigning items to behavior-derived parent/child sets or fixing one graph partition cell as the first token, this builds behavior-defined sectors of the first-level codebook and uses a behavior-conditioned radial coordinate in hyperbolic space to choose among codes inside a sector. The behavior signal changes the point being quantized, not merely the candidate set or an auxiliary loss.
ideas.observables: Record first-level assignment changes, first-token next-item predictability and prefix behavior statistics, level-three distinct triples, finite gradient/update statistics, and frozen Stage3 test Recall@10. The behavioral diagnostics do not decide admission; Recall@10 is the judgement.
risks: Sparse item transition profiles may be dominated by the pseudocount or popularity; KL sectors may not align with predictive prefixes; adding a behavior vector may distort semantic reconstruction; sector code allocation can starve rare sectors; curved assignment may provide no gain. The fixed topology also cannot adapt if training behaviors shift during optimization.
ideas.safeguards: Store profiles sparsely; define q for zero-outdegree items as p; normalize distributions with a 1e−12 floor; normalize behavior prototypes and use FP32. Use an orthonormal PCA projection and a training-latent median with 1e−12 floor. Clamp κ||x||² and κ||v||² to at most 1−1e−5, clamp acosh argument to ≥1, clamp atanh arguments where exp/log maps require them, and fail fast on nonfinite distances. Empty sectors are omitted; deterministic smallest-index ties and largest-remainder tie breaks; do not merge residual levels or postprocess away third-level identity.
ideas.spec_equations: n_ij=Σ_{u,t}1[i_{u,t}=i,i_{u,t+1}=j]; p_j=Σ_i n_ij/Σ_{i,j}n_ij; q_ij=(n_ij+p_j)/(out_i+1); g_i=argmin_g KL(q_i||μ_g); a_g=largest_remainder(K0·N_g/N), min 1; h_i=PCA(μ_{g_i})·median_j||z_j||; y_i=z_i+h_i; s=1/median_i||y_i||; κ=1/median_i||s y_i||²; c1_i=argmin_{k∈C_{g_i}} [acosh(1+2κ||x_i−v_k||²/((1−κ||x_i||²)(1−κ||v_k||²)))/sqrt(κ)]², x_i=exp_0^{−κ}(s y_i), v_k=exp_0^{−κ}(s e_k); r_i=z_i−e_{c1_i}; (c2,c3)=baseline_RQ(r_i). Use deterministic clustering/ties; constants α=1 and G=ceil(sqrt(K0)) are fixed documented rules, not tuned.
ideas.spec_inputs_outputs: Inputs: Stage2 training sequences, training item embeddings, batch encoder latents z, configured first-level codebook size K0, trainable first-level prototypes, and baseline residual quantizers. Outputs: frozen item sector labels and code allocation; first-level assignments and quantization values; residual levels 2/3; full SIDs.

specification.text: For each training item i compute successor distribution q_i[j]=(n_ij+α p[j])/(out_i+α), where n_ij counts adjacent training-only transitions, p is the training-only successor marginal, and α=1 is a documented unit pseudocount. Set sector prototypes μ_g by deterministic spherical k-means on q_i, with G=min(K0, ceil(sqrt(K0))) sectors; assign each item g(i)=argmin_g KL(q_i||μ_g). Allocate K0 first-level IDs to sectors by largest-remainder rounding of their training item counts, enforcing one per nonempty sector. Define behavior-conditioned latent y_i=z_i+μ_g(i) projected to the encoder latent dimension by a fixed seeded PCA fitted only on training items (if dimensions already match, use identity); normalize μ to unit norm and scale it by median training ||z||. Assign c1(i)=argmin_{k∈C_g(i)} d_{-κ}(exp_0(s y_i),exp_0(s e_k))². Subtract the selected Euclidean prototype from z_i and quantize residual levels 2 and 3 with the baseline RQ-VAE. κ=1/median(||s y||²) over training items, clamped to finite positive values, makes curvature scale-relative rather than tuned.

Our analysis reveals that restricted initialization and limited encoder capacity result in tokens collapse and embeddings collapse. Building on these findings, we propose potential solutions aimed at mitigating each collapse. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive study examining representation collapsing problems in vector quantization.

papers.abstract: Machine learning algorithms have been shown to be highly effective in solving optimization problems in a wide range of applications. Such algorithms typically use gradient descent with backpropagation and the chain rule. Hence, the backpropagation fails if intermediate gradients are zero for some functions in the computational graph, because it causes the gradients to collapse when multiplying with zero. Vector quantization is one of those challenging functions for machine learning algorithms, since it is a piece-wise constant function and its gradient is zero almost everywhere. A typical solution is to apply the straight through estimator which simply copies the gradients over the vector quantization function in the backpropagation. Other solutions are based on smooth or stochastic approximation. This study proposes a vector quantization technique called NSVQ, which approximates the vector quantization behavior by substituting a multiplicative noise so that it can be used for machine learning problems. Specifically, the vector quantization error is replaced by product of the original error and a normalized noise vector, the samples of which are drawn from a zero-mean, unit-varianc
